body:
What is a stepwell?

A stepwell is a water structure in which a series of steps allows people to descend from ground level towards a well or underground water source. In Gujarat, a stepwell is commonly called a vav. The terms baoli and baori are also used for stepwells in other parts of India.

Unlike an ordinary well, where water is generally drawn from the surface using a rope or another lifting device, a stepwell provides access to lower levels through stairways. As the groundwater level changes with the seasons, people can descend further to reach accessible water, provided that the well continues to contain water.

Stepwell

A stepwell is a subterranean water-access structure combining a well with descending steps. Larger examples may also contain landings, pillared pavilions, galleries and richly carved architectural surfaces.

Why did stepwells develop in Gujarat?

Gujarat experiences a strongly seasonal rainfall pattern. Much of its annual rainfall occurs during the monsoon, while the remaining months can be comparatively dry. Historically, communities needed dependable ways to obtain and preserve access to water during periods of scarcity.

Stepwells addressed this need by providing access to groundwater. Rainwater could replenish groundwater through infiltration, but a stepwell was not simply an open tank designed to collect rainfall. Its usefulness depended on local groundwater conditions, the depth of the well and the maintenance of the structure.

The tradition became particularly important in Gujarat and Rajasthan. Over time, simple stepped arrangements developed into elaborate underground buildings containing several storeys, platforms and ornamental sculptures.

Water architecture served several purposes

Water supply

The principal practical purpose was to provide access to water for residents and travellers. Descending steps made it possible to approach water at different depths rather than relying entirely on lifting it from ground level.

Resting and gathering places

Large stepwells contained shaded spaces where people could rest, meet and seek relief from the heat. Travellers and merchants could use such structures along established routes. Their public character made them important parts of settlement life.

Religious and charitable significance

Water was associated with purification, prosperity and sacredness. Consequently, several stepwells were decorated with images of deities, auspicious symbols and mythological scenes. Providing water was also regarded as a charitable act.

Rulers, queens, wealthy merchants and other donors therefore supported the construction of wells and water structures. Their patronage could combine public welfare, religious merit, remembrance and the demonstration of prosperity.

Stepwells, ordinary wells and stepped tanks

These structures are related because all provide access to water, but they should not be treated as identical.

  • Ordinary well: Primarily a vertical shaft from which water can be drawn, often from ground level.
  • Stepwell or vav: A well reached through descending steps, sometimes with multiple underground storeys and pavilions.
  • Stepped tank or kund: An open water basin with steps arranged along its sides. The Surya Kund at Modhera is a Gujarat example.

The distinction is architectural rather than religious. A stepwell may contain sacred sculptures, while a stepped tank may form part of a temple complex. Neither religious decoration nor the presence of steps alone establishes that a structure is a vav.

Prelims focus

  • The Gujarati term for a stepwell is vav.
  • Baoli and baori are other regional terms for stepwells.
  • Stepwells provide access to groundwater through descending stairways.
  • Major functions included water access, public rest, social gathering and religious or charitable activity.
  • Trap: Every stepped water structure is not necessarily a stepwell. An open stepped tank is architecturally different from a vav with a well shaft.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, chapter 5, Rulers and Buildings, printed pp. 61–65; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 75–76; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Rani-ki-Vav at Patan, Gujarat, Description and Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 23 November 2026.]

title: Stepwells of Gujarat: Water Supply, Public Life and Sacred Space

body:
The essential parts of a developed stepwell

Large stepwells required careful architectural planning because their buildings extended below ground level. The structure had to provide access to water while supporting stone platforms, staircases, galleries and the surrounding earth.

Descending staircase

The staircase connects the ground-level entrance to progressively lower parts of the structure. A long stepped corridor may contain intermediate platforms or landings, allowing people to pause while descending or ascending.

Landings and pillared pavilions

A pavilion is a covered or partially open architectural space. In a large vav, pavilions commonly contain pillars supporting beams and upper floors. They interrupt the long descent and create usable spaces at different levels.

The number and arrangement of pavilions differ between monuments. A stepwell does not need to have a fixed number of storeys to qualify as a vav.

Well shaft and water-access area

The well shaft is the deeper, generally vertical portion associated with groundwater. In elaborate stepwells, the descending corridor may lead to a tank-like water-access area near the shaft. Water could also be drawn using suitable lifting arrangements.

The water level was not necessarily constant. Seasonal changes could expose or submerge different parts of the lower structure.

How did the underground structure remain usable?

Structural support

Stone columns, beams, platforms and supporting walls helped distribute the loads of the building. These components had to support the underground galleries while resisting pressure from the surrounding ground.

Medieval Indian builders commonly used trabeate construction, in which horizontal beams rest upon vertical supports such as pillars. Corbelled construction, involving successive projecting stone courses, was another historical building technique.

These techniques were used in temples and buildings associated with stepped wells. Later architecture also incorporated other structural forms, including arches. The presence of decorative arch-shaped carving alone does not establish that a true load-bearing arch was used.

Light and ventilation

Openings above staircases, landings and galleries allowed daylight and air to enter the underground spaces. At the same time, the surrounding masonry and limited direct sunlight helped create shaded interiors.

The resulting cooler environment made many stepwells useful resting places during hot weather. The actual temperature difference depended on the structure and conditions; it was not a fixed property of every vav.

Stone construction and carving

Stone was used for pillars, beams, stairways and decorative surfaces. Sculptors created intricate designs by removing material with cutting and chiselling tools.

Relief sculpture is carving that projects from a background surface. Many images on stepwell walls and pillars are reliefs, whereas a fully three-dimensional sculpture can be viewed from all sides.

Builders and sculptors therefore needed both engineering and artistic skills. Structural members supported the monument, while carved surfaces expressed the religious and cultural ideas of its patrons.

Structure and decoration perform different roles

A pillar may be a structural support and also carry decorative sculpture. The carved figure is not itself the reason the building remains stable; the supporting stone member performs that engineering function.

Prelims focus

  • A developed vav may contain a stepped corridor, landings, pavilions, a water-access area and a well shaft.
  • Trabeate construction: Horizontal beams supported by vertical columns or walls.
  • Relief sculpture: A figure or design carved in projection from a background.
  • Openings provide light and ventilation to underground galleries.
  • Different vavs can have different numbers of storeys and different structural arrangements.
  • Trap: An underground pavilion is not the same component as the vertical well shaft.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, chapter 5, Rulers and Buildings, printed pp. 61–63, Engineering Skills and Construction; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Stone, printed pp. 27–29; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Rani-ki-Vav at Patan, Gujarat, Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, Adalaj ni Vav, About the Location, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The principal structural elements of a developed Gujarat stepwell.

title: Engineering of a Vav: Stairways, Pavilions, Wells and Stone Construction

body:
Location and historical background

Rani-ki-Vav, meaning the Queen's Stepwell, is located at Patan in Gujarat, on the banks of the Saraswati River.

It belongs to the 11th century CE and is associated with the Chaulukya or Solanki dynasty, which ruled significant parts of Gujarat during the medieval period. Patan, historically known as Anahilavada or Anhilwad Patan, was an important capital of this dynasty.

The monument is traditionally attributed to Queen Udayamati, the wife of King Bhimdev I. She is credited with commissioning the stepwell in memory of her husband.

A medieval literary tradition recorded by the Jain author Merutunga in the Prabandhachintamani associates the monument with Udayamati. Gujarat Tourism commonly dates its commissioning to 1063 CE. The broader historical identification is that it is an 11th-century memorial stepwell.

Patronage

Rani-ki-Vav is associated with Queen Udayamati and was constructed in memory of her husband, Bhimdev I, of the Chaulukya or Solanki dynasty.

Maru-Gurjara architectural style

Rani-ki-Vav is an outstanding example of Maru-Gurjara architecture, a medieval architectural tradition strongly associated with western India, especially Gujarat and Rajasthan.

The style is distinguished by refined stone construction, carefully proportioned architectural spaces, elaborate columns and richly sculpted surfaces. At Rani-ki-Vav, these qualities appear in an underground monument rather than only in an above-ground temple.

The stepwell demonstrates that architectural achievements of the Solanki period were not confined to temples. Sophisticated techniques and artistic traditions were also applied to public water structures.

Arrangement of the stepwell

Rani-ki-Vav extends along an east–west axis. The stepped passage begins at the eastern side, while the well shaft lies at the western end.

Its major architectural components include:

  • A long descending stepped corridor.
  • 7 levels of stairs and sculptural panels in the original design.
  • A sequence of 4 pillared pavilions of increasing height towards the well.
  • A lower rectangular water-access tank.
  • A deep well shaft at the western end.

The descending spaces contain decorated columns, niches and wall panels. Their arrangement combines practical access to water with an exceptionally elaborate architectural experience.

The meaning of its 7 levels

The frequently mentioned 7 levels refer to the monument's original arrangement of descending stairs and sculptured storeys. They should not be interpreted as 7 fully preserved, independent buildings.

Parts of the original pavilions have been lost or damaged, although the overall architectural arrangement remains recognizable.

Prelims focus

  • Location: Patan, Gujarat, on the Saraswati River.
  • Period: 11th century CE.
  • Patron: Queen Udayamati, wife of Bhimdev I.
  • Dynasty: Chaulukya or Solanki.
  • Architecture: Maru-Gurjara style, with 7 descending levels and 4 principal pavilions.
  • Trap: The well shaft is at the western end; the long stepped approach extends along an east–west axis.

[References: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Rani-ki-Vav at Patan, Gujarat, Description and Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 23 November 2026; Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, Rani-ki-Vav Patan Gujarat, monument description, consulted 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, Rani Ki Vav, About the Location and Brief History, consulted 23 November 2026; Sahapedia, The Rani ki Vav Stepwell at Patan, Gujarat, discussion of historical patronage and Merutunga's account, consulted 23 November 2026.]

body:
Why is Rani-ki-Vav called an inverted temple?

Rani-ki-Vav is often described as an inverted temple because its elaborate architectural and sculptural spaces descend into the earth towards water instead of rising upwards as a conventional temple superstructure.

The expression highlights the sacred significance attached to water. A visitor descended through richly carved architectural spaces towards the lower water-access area.

It does not mean that Rani-ki-Vav is literally an upside-down replica of a particular temple. The description expresses the combination of sacred symbolism with a functional underground water structure.

The sculptural programme

The monument contains an exceptionally extensive collection of carved images. According to the UNESCO World Heritage description, the stepwell has more than 500 principal sculptures and over 1,000 minor sculptures.

The sculptural programme includes religious, mythological and secular subjects. Images appear on the walls, niches, pillars and other architectural surfaces.

Vishnu and the Dashavatara tradition

A major theme is Vishnu and his various manifestations. The Dashavatara refers to the traditional group of 10 principal incarnations of Vishnu.

Several carvings at the monument depict Vishnu in different forms. The presence of these images makes Vaishnava iconography particularly important for identifying its sculptural themes.

Sheshashayi Vishnu

One of the most distinctive images is Sheshashayi Vishnu, also called Sheshashayana Vishnu. This representation depicts Vishnu reclining upon the serpent Shesha or Ananta.

The image is associated with cosmic rest and the continuity of creation. At Rani-ki-Vav, its placement in the lower part of the structure reinforces the religious significance of the descent towards water.

Apsaras and other sculptural subjects

The monument also contains images of apsaras, traditionally understood as celestial female figures, alongside other divine figures, mythological subjects and decorative representations.

Some figures are shown performing everyday actions, such as attending to their appearance. These details demonstrate the breadth of subjects represented by the sculptors.

Geometric and ornamental carving

Religious figures are accompanied by elaborate geometric patterns, floral decoration and stylized animal forms. These designs help organize the carved surfaces and enrich the visual character of the monument.

The precision of the carvings shows the close relationship between architecture and sculpture in the western Indian tradition.

Function and symbolism together

Rani-ki-Vav illustrates how a practical public structure could also express religious beliefs and the memory of its patron. Its importance does not come exclusively from its sculptures or exclusively from its water system. The unusual achievement lies in combining both purposes within a single architectural composition.

Two important descriptions

  • Maru-Gurjara: The architectural style of the monument.
  • Inverted temple: A description of its descending sacred architectural composition and the sanctity associated with water.

Prelims focus

  • Vishnu and the Dashavatara are major sculptural themes at Rani-ki-Vav.
  • Sheshashayi Vishnu represents Vishnu reclining on Shesha or Ananta.
  • Apsaras and other religious, mythological and secular figures also appear.
  • UNESCO describes more than 500 principal sculptures and over 1,000 minor sculptures.
  • The expression inverted temple emphasizes the sacred significance of water and the descending architectural arrangement.
  • Trap: Inverted temple is an architectural interpretation, not the name of a separate temple located inside the stepwell.

[References: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Rani-ki-Vav at Patan, Gujarat, Description and Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 23 November 2026; Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, Rani-ki-Vav Patan Gujarat, description of sculptures and Vishnu iconography, consulted 23 November 2026; UNESCO, Rani-ki-Vav (The Queen's Stepwell), 18 July 2024, updated 15 November 2024, architectural and sculptural description.]
